Uncleanness
un-klēn'nes
n. (ceremonial or moral impurity; rendering Hebrew tumah, Greek akatharsia)
From unclean, Saxon unclaene, with the ending -ness. Hebrew tumah is ritual defilement, a state rather than an act — a man became unclean by contact with death, disease, or discharge, and could not approach the sanctuary until cleansed, whether or not he had sinned.

Biblical Definition

Uncleanness in Scripture begins as a ceremonial category and becomes a moral one, and the two are connected by design. Under the law a man could be unclean without being guilty — by touching a corpse, by childbirth, by disease — and the point of the system was not hygiene but instruction: God is holy, death and corruption cannot come near him, and access requires cleansing. The stakes are stated bluntly: “Thus shall ye separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness; that they die not in their uncleanness, when they defile my tabernacle that is among them” (Leviticus 15:31). The New Testament carries the word over to moral defilement, chiefly sexual. Paul lists it among the sins not even to be named among saints: “fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints” (Ephesians 5:3), and states the alternative in a sentence: “God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness” (1 Thessalonians 4:7). Romans makes uncleanness itself a judgment: “God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts” (Romans 1:24) — the giving-up is the penalty, and the sin is its own punishment.

Webster 1828 Definition

Impurity — ceremonial under the law, moral in the New Testament. The Levitical system taught that corruption cannot approach a holy God; Paul says God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness.

expand to see more

UNCLEANNESS, n. [from unclean.] Foulness; dirtiness; filthiness.

2. Want of ritual or ceremonial purity, under the Levitical law.

3. Moral impurity; defilement by sin; especially, lewdness; unchastity.

4. In Scripture, that they die not in their uncleanness, Lev. 15.

5. God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness, 1 Thess. 4.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 15:31 — "Thus shall ye separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness; that they die not in their uncleanness, when they defile my tabernacle that is among them."

Ephesians 5:3 — "But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints;"

1 Thessalonians 4:7 — "For God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness."

Romans 1:24 — "Wherefore God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts, to dishonour their own bodies between themselves:"

Modern Corruption

Sexual purity is presented as a private preference or an outdated restriction, and the very notion of defilement is treated as shaming. Scripture makes purity a matter of the call of God and locates the defilement in the heart.

expand to see more

The modern position holds that consensual conduct cannot defile anyone, and that language of uncleanness is itself the harm. Scripture's answer is not primarily about consequences but about calling: God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness. The Christian sexual ethic is not a set of restrictions attached to an otherwise neutral life; it follows from what a believer has been called and joined to, which is why Paul argues from the body being the temple of the Holy Ghost rather than from harm.

Romans 1:24 supplies the point most often missed in these debates. Paul does not present uncleanness merely as an offence that will be judged later; he presents God's giving men up to it as itself a judgment now. A society progressively unable to see anything wrong is not escaping the verdict but experiencing it. The principle to recover is that the Levitical system was teaching all along what the gospel then answers: the unclean cannot approach, and the remedy is a cleansing God provides — the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tumah is ritual uncleanness, from tame, to be defiled; taher is to be clean. Greek akatharsia is impurity, from a- and kathairo, to cleanse — the root of English catharsis.

expand to see more

Hebrew tumah (H2932) — ritual uncleanness, defilement; a state barring approach to the sanctuary.

Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be or become unclean; the verb of Levitical defilement.

Hebrew taher (H2891) — to be clean, to purify; create in me a clean heart, O God.

Greek akatharsia (G167) — uncleanness, impurity; listed with fornication in Ephesians 5:3.

Greek hagiasmos (G38) — sanctification, holiness; the alternative named in 1 Thessalonians 4:7.

Usage

"Of the seriousness of ceremonial defilement: that they die not in their uncleanness (Leviticus 15:31)."

"Of what is not to be named among saints: fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness (Ephesians 5:3)."

"Of uncleanness as itself a judgment: God also gave them up to uncleanness (Romans 1:24)."
